scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

This creates an imbalance where you’re consistently giving up your rights for her convenience. - By refusing to comply with her last-minute changes (e.g., the lake trip, amusement park, 4th of July party), you’re enforcing the *legal* schedule, which is a reasonable boundary. Consistency in parenting time is crucial for children’s stability and your rights as a parent. 2. **Child’s Best Interests** - While your ex frames her actions as "for your son," the cumulative effect of her flexibility has likely left *you* with less time than agreed. Children thrive on routine and predictability. Your son may feel confused or resentful if he perceives one parent as "more important" due to unequal access. - Keeping him during her scheduled time (e.g., the 4th of July party) isn’t inherently wrong if it’s a one-time enforcement of the schedule. However, if this becomes a pattern, it could strain co-parenting further. 3. **Power Dynamics & Manipulation** - Your ex’s use of phrases like *"it’s for your son"* is a classic emotional manipulation tactic. Parents often weaponize guilt, especially when one parent feels "less capable" (e.g., due to work, distance, or perceived "less involvement"). - You’re right to question whether her "flexibility" is truly for the child or her own needs. A healthy co-parenting relationship requires mutual respect for the *legal* agreement, not just emotional appeals. 4. **Legal Perspective** - Courts typically expect parents to honor visitation schedules unless there’s a valid reason (e.g., illness, emergency). If your ex has a history of altering the schedule without justification, you may have grounds to request modifications through the court. Documenting these incidents (texts, emails) could help if you pursue enforcement. - **Key question:** Is this a one-time enforcement, or are you setting a precedent? If you’re doing this repeatedly, it could escalate conflict. If it’s a response to a pattern of disrespect, it may be justified. 5. **Psychological Impact** - Children often pick up on parental tension. If they sense one parent is "more important" due to unequal time, it can create loyalty conflicts or anxiety. However, if your son is old enough (8 years), he may understand that both parents deserve fair time. - Your frustration is valid—parental alienation (even unintentional) can harm the child’s relationship with *both* parents. Your goal should be to protect your bond with him, not undermine hers. --- ### **Is This "AITA"?** **It depends on context, but here’s a nuanced answer:** - **Not AITA** if: - This is a *one-time* enforcement of the schedule due to her repeated disrespect (e.g., skipping your time for her family’s plans). - You’ve documented her pattern of altering the schedule without valid reasons. - You’re not using this as an excuse to withhold time indefinitely (e.g., "I’ll only give him back if she changes the schedule"). - **Could be AITA** if: - You’re making this a habit (e.g., refusing to return him for *every* minor inconvenience). - Your actions are retaliatory (e.g., you’re not open to negotiating fair solutions). - You’re using the child as a pawn in your conflict (e.g., threatening to withhold him unless she changes the schedule permanently). --- ### **Recommended Steps:** 1. **Document Everything** - Save texts, emails, and any evidence of her breaking the schedule. This is critical if you need to go to court. 2. **Communicate Clearly (Without Emotion)** - Instead of arguing, try a neutral message like: *"I understand you have plans, but the schedule is set for [date/time]. If we can’t meet at the usual drop-off, we’ll need to adjust it legally. Otherwise, I’ll follow the court order."* - Avoid ultimatums (e.g., "I’m keeping him until you change the schedule"), as this can escalate conflict. 3. **Propose a Fair Compromise** - Suggest swapping weekends *once* to make up for lost time, but tie it to her respecting the schedule moving forward. Example: *"If we can agree to swap this weekend so I get my full time, can we also agree to stick to the schedule next time?"* 4. **Consider Mediation or Legal Review** - If she continues to ignore the schedule, consult a family lawyer to discuss modifying the agreement. Courts may adjust schedules if one parent is consistently taking advantage of the system. 5. **Focus on Your Son** - Reassure him that both parents love him and that the schedule is fair. Avoid badmouthing his mother, even in frustration. Frame it as *"Mom and Dad both want to spend time with you, and we’re figuring out how to make that work."* 6. **Protect Your Own Well-Being** - Co-parenting with someone who manipulates can be exhausting. Set boundaries—you’re not obligated to accommodate her at the expense of your own mental health or legal rights. --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re not the "asshole" for prioritizing your scheduled time, especially after years of her bending the rules. However, the *how* matters. If you handle this with calm, clear communication (and not emotional outbursts), you’re more likely to maintain a functional co-parenting relationship. If she continues to defy the schedule, you may need legal intervention to enforce fairness. Would you like help drafting a text to her to set boundaries? Or are you looking for strategies to handle future conflicts?
